title: Date and publication
short: Written in the trenches about June 1916 and published in Poetry (Chicago) in December 1916; Rosenberg was killed on 1 April 1918.
body: Rosenberg, a Jewish painter-poet from London's East End, enlisted in 1915 and served as a private. The Oxford archive dates the first typescript to June 1916. He sent the poem to Edward Marsh in August 1916, describing it as simple as ordinary talk, and to Gordon Bottomley (whose transcript preserves a variant); Harriet Monroe received it in October 1916 and printed it in Poetry in December 1916. The title names the dawn 'stand-to', when soldiers manned the parapet against attack. Fussell ranked it the greatest poem of the war, and its free verse and casual tone set it apart from much patriotic verse of 1914-16.

title: The crumbling darkness
short: Dawn is imagined as something solid breaking up, like earth or a trench wall.
body: Rosenberg's verb gives darkness texture, as if it were the soil of the trench falling away. Dawn was the most dangerous hour on the Western Front, the time of stand-to and of attacks. Fussell placed the poem within the tradition of the dawn song, the aubade, which the war made ironic: daybreak brings not the parting of lovers but the threat of death.

title: 'druid Time'
greek: Latin druides, from a Celtic word
short: Time as a druid: a pagan priest of sacrifice, ancient and unchanged. Rosenberg admitted the line might seem vague.
body: Classical writers describe the druids of Gaul and Britain as priests who performed human sacrifice (Caesar, Gallic War 6.16), so 'druid Time' suggests an ancient power that demands victims, now as always. The phrase also recalls Stonehenge, which popular belief linked with druids, and so the sense of dawn over old stones. In his letter to Marsh, Rosenberg said the second line might seem vague and that he meant it to give the sense of dawn. Critics differ over how heavily to load the image with sacrifice.

anchor: a live thing leaps my hand
title: 'leaps my hand'
short: The verb is transitive: the rat jumps over the poet's hand. 'Only' sets one live thing against a landscape of the dead.
body: 'Leap' with a direct object (leap a fence, leap a ditch) is long-established English usage recorded in the OED. 'Only a live thing' stresses that the one obviously living creature in the trench at dawn is the rat; the soldiers appear later as 'strong eyes, fine limbs' whose hold on life is less secure than the animal's. The leap is the first action of the poem, abrupt and unexpected after the slow dawn of the opening lines.

title: 'sardonic'
short: The rat seems to mock the soldiers. 'Sardonic' comes from the Greek name for a bitter, grimacing laugh.
body: Greek sardanios, later sardonios, describes a bitter or scornful smile; Odysseus smiles 'sardonically' at Odyssey 20.302, and ancient writers derived the word from a Sardinian plant whose poison drew the face into a grin. Rats swarmed in the trenches, feeding on the dead, and were loathed by soldiers. Fussell observes that Rosenberg's rat, the natural emblem of the demonic, turns out charming and worldly, and seems to wonder at the terror of men. The tone of 'queer' and 'droll' is affectionate.

title: The parapet's poppy
short: The speaker picks a poppy growing on the trench parapet and sticks it behind his ear, a gesture of levity.
body: The parapet is the bank of earth on the enemy side of a trench. Fussell reads the poppy as a flower fed by the dead, and the picked flower as already doomed. By 1916 the poppy was linked with the war dead through John McCrae's 'In Flanders Fields' (Punch, December 1915), but Rosenberg's poppy is first a casual decoration, before the poem draws its blood meaning out.

title: 'cosmopolitan sympathies'
short: The rat is a citizen of the world, loyal to no nation; some readers hear also the slur used against Jews.
body: Greek kosmopolites, 'citizen of the world', was the Cynic Diogenes' answer when asked where he came from (Diogenes Laertius 6.63). The rat crosses between English and German lines without national feeling, which is why 'they would shoot you if they knew'. Some readers point out that 'cosmopolitan' was used to accuse Jews of rootless, divided loyalty, and that Rosenberg, a Jewish private who met prejudice in the army, may be wryly identifying with the rat. Critics differ on how far to press this; the main sense is the absurdity of national hatred.

title: The parenthesis
short: A wry aside: the rat's dislikes are as unknowable as its loyalties. The line is in the early version but absent from the 1916 printing.
body: The parenthesis matches 'sympathies' with its opposite and keeps the tone of half-joking talk. The Oxford hypermedia edition records that the line stands in the version Rosenberg wrote before June 1916 but was dropped from the printed text, so students should check which version an edition follows. The archive text includes the line. The aside also widens the joke: if the rat's sympathies are cosmopolitan, its dislikes are probably just as indiscriminate, and so, implicitly, are the hatreds of the human armies on either side.

title: English hand, German hand
short: The rat touches both armies, linking enemies in one touch, as Donne's flea mingles two lovers' blood.
body: The rat makes a bodily connection between the speaker and an unknown German soldier, and the poem's sympathy flows through the animal to the enemy. The Oxford annotation compares Donne's 'The Flea', in which an insect joins two bodies, and notes the Metaphysical poets' influence on Rosenberg. The idea of shared humanity across the lines returns in Owen's 'Strange Meeting'.

title: 'the sleeping green between'
short: No man's land between the trenches, quiet at dawn; the pastoral word 'green' makes it a village green.
body: No man's land was often mud and wire, but in a quiet sector at dawn it could look green and still. 'Green' suggests the English village green and pastoral; the Oxford edition compares Blake's 'The Ecchoing Green'. Fussell made the poem a central instance of soldiers' pastoral, in which images of the English countryside serve as an ironic counterpoint to the front.

title: 'inwardly grin'
short: The speaker imagines the rat secretly amused at the human spectacle.
body: The Oxford edition notes that 'inwardly' is absent from the earliest version, which shows Rosenberg refining the tone of the rat's mockery. The grin connects back to 'sardonic', the grimace of bitter laughter. The rat's mocking survival sets up the reversal of the next lines, in which the splendid human bodies are 'less chanced than you for life', that is, with less chance of surviving than the rat.

title: 'haughty athletes'
short: The young soldiers as fine bodies, glancing at the athletic-heroic ideal of 1914 verse.
body: The list praises the soldiers as physical specimens, in the sporting language that recruitment and early war poetry applied to young men (Rupert Brooke's 1914 sonnets idealise the young dead). Rosenberg, a working-class Jew from the East End and a reluctant soldier, stands at an angle to that ideal: 'haughty' is admiring and ironic at once. Silkin reads Rosenberg's war poems as refusing both patriotic idealism and simple protest.

sources.cite: Jon Silkin, Out of Battle: The Poetry of the Great War (Oxford UP, 1972)

anchor: Bonds to the whims of murder
title: 'Bonds'
short: Bondsmen or slaves: the soldiers are bound over to the arbitrary chances of killing.
body: 'Bond' in the old sense of a serf or slave (bondman) is recorded by the OED, and the word also suggests a legal pledge. Either way the soldiers' lives belong to chance ('whims') and to 'murder', a strong word for battle. The next lines show the result: bodies 'sprawled in the bowels of the earth'. The abstract, Latinate phrasing contrasts with the colloquial address to the rat.

title: 'the bowels of the earth'
short: The trenches, shell-holes and graves as the inside of the earth's body.
body: The phrase is proverbial (Shakespeare's Hotspur reports a fop's complaint about saltpetre dug 'out of the bowels of the harmless earth', 1 Henry IV 1.3), but here it is literal: men lie in dug earth, dead or alive. 'The torn fields of France' makes the landscape a wounded body, preparing for the poppies 'whose roots are in man's veins'. The grotesque bodily metaphor is typical of Rosenberg.

title: 'shrieking iron and flame'
short: Shells and fire hurled through a still sky: the only direct picture of bombardment in the poem.
body: The Oxford edition reports that an earlier draft had a different passage at this point, including a line about 'a shell's haphazard fury'; the revision replaces it with the shrieking iron and flame. The speaker asks what the rat sees in the soldiers' eyes: what 'quaver', what heart 'aghast'. The 'still heavens' set the calm dawn sky against the violence that passes through it. The question is unanswered; the poem turns at once to the poppies.

anchor: Poppies whose roots are in man
title: Poppies rooted in veins
short: The poppies feed on the dead: their roots reach into men's blood, drawing on the belief that the flowers were red with soldiers' blood.
body: Poppies flourished in the churned ground of Flanders and France, and the popular notion that they drew their colour from the dead was widespread. Silkin argues that Rosenberg takes up this common belief and renews it. 'Drop, and are ever dropping' fuses flowers and men: poppies shed their petals, soldiers fall continuously. The poppy is also the classical flower of sleep and oblivion.

anchor: a little white with the dust
title: 'a little white with the dust'
short: The poet's poppy is 'safe' but whitened by dust, a sign of fading and of the speaker's own danger.
body: Fussell calls 'safe' the poem's most ironic word, since the flower's apparent safety is illusory. The white dust of the hot summer of 1916 drains the red flower, a small foretaste of death. The Oxford edition reports Silkin's hearing of 'a little while' behind 'a little white', a little while, so that the poppy and the man survive only briefly. The understatement of the last line shows Rosenberg's control of tone.
